**Prince Alexander Mikhailovich Gorchakov** (Russian: Алекса́ндр Миха́йлович Горчако́в; 15 July 1798 – 11 March 1883[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Gorchakov#cite_note-1)) was a Russian diplomat and statesman from the Gorchakov princely family. He has an enduring reputation as one of the most influential and respected diplomats of the mid-19th century.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Gorchakov#cite_note-2) Scholars agree that the termination of the demilitarisation of the Black Sea was Gorchakov's greatest accomplishment but add that he stayed too long as foreign minister.

## Early life and career
[edit]
Gorchakov was born at Haapsalu, Governorate of Estonia, and was educated at the Tsarskoye Selo Lyceum, where he had the poet Alexander Pushkin as a school-fellow. He became a good classical scholar, and learned to speak and write in French with facility and elegance. Pushkin in one of his poems described young Gorchakov as _Fortune's favoured son_, and predicted his success.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Gorchakov#cite_note-EB1911-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Gorchakov#cite_note-4)
On leaving the lyceum Gorchakov entered the foreign office under Count Nesselrode. His first diplomatic work of importance was the negotiation of a marriage between the Grand Duchess Olga and the crown prince Charles of Württemberg. He remained at Stuttgart for some years as Russian minister and confidential adviser of the crown princess. He foretold the outbreak of the revolutionary spirit in Germany and Austria, and was credited with counselling the abdication of Ferdinand I of Austria in favour of Francis Joseph. When the German Confederation was re-established in 1850 in place of the Frankfurt Parliament, Gorchakov was appointed Russian minister to the diet. It was here that he first met Count Bismarck, with whom he formed a friendship which was afterwards renewed at St Petersburg.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Gorchakov#cite_note-EB1911-3)

## Early life and career
The Emperor Nicholas found that his ambassador at Vienna, Baron Meyendorff, was not a sympathetic instrument for carrying out his schemes in the East. He therefore transferred Gorchakov to Vienna, where the latter remained through the critical period of the Crimean War. Gorchakov perceived that Russian designs against the Ottoman Empire, which was supported by Britain and France, were impracticable, and he counselled Russia to make no more useless sacrifices, but to accept the basis of a pacification. At the same time, although he attended the Paris conference of 1856, he purposely abstained from affixing his signature to the treaty of peace after that of Count Alexey Fyodorovich Orlov, Russia's chief representative. For the time, however, he made a virtue of necessity, and Alexander II, recognising the wisdom and courage which Gorchakov had exhibited, appointed him minister of foreign affairs in place of Count Nesselrode.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Gorchakov#cite_note-EB1911-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Gorchakov#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Gorchakov#cite_note-6)

## Minister of foreign affairs
[edit]
Not long after his accession to office, Gorchakov issued a circular to the foreign powers in which he announced that Russia proposed, for internal reasons, to keep herself as free as possible from complications abroad, and he added the now-historic phrase, _La Russie ne boude pas; elle se recueille_ ('Russia is not sulking, she is composing herself'). During the January Uprising in Congress Poland, Gorchakov rebuffed the suggestions of Britain, Austria and France for assuaging the severities employed in quelling it, and he was especially acrid in his replies to Earl Russell's despatches. The Prussian support was assured by the Alvensleben Convention. In July 1863 Gorchakov was appointed Chancellor of the Russian Empire, expressly in reward for his bold diplomatic attitude towards an indignant Europe. The appointment was hailed with enthusiasm in Russia.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Gorchakov#cite_note-EB1911-3)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Gorchakov#cite_note-%D0%AD%D0%A1%D0%91%D0%AD-7)
A rapprochement now began between the courts of Russia and Prussia, and in 1863, Gorchakov smoothed the way for the occupation of Schleswig-Holstein by German troops. That seemed equally favourable to Austria and Prussia, but it was the latter power that gained all the substantial advantages. When conflict arose between Austria and Prussia in 1866, Russia remained neutral and permitted Prussia to reap the benefits arising from the conflict and establish its supremacy in Germany.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Gorchakov#cite_note-EB1911-3)
In 1867 Russia and the United States concluded the sale of Alaska, a process which had begun as early as 1854 during the Crimean War. Gorchakov was not against the sale but always advocated for careful and secret negotiations and saw the eventuality of the sale but not the immediate necessity._[citation needed_]

When the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–1871 broke out, Russia argued for the neutrality of Austria-Hungary. However, the cordial relations between the cabinets of Saint Petersburg and Berlin did not last much longer.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Gorchakov#cite_note-EB1911-3)

A Russian diplomat who rivaled Otto von Bismarck in the mid-19th century. He was a cousin of Mikhail Dmitrievich Gorchakov, the commander-in-chief of the Russian Southern Front during the
Crimean War
. Raised in Western-style salons in Saint Petersburg, he was a classmate of the poet Alexander Pushkin in his youth, who foresaw in his poetry that he would achieve greatness. He entered the diplomatic service in 1817 and attended international congresses in Troppau, Verona, and Laibach as a member of the official Russian delegation from 1820 to 1822. Despite efforts by Foreign Minister Count Karl Robert Nesselrode to block his promotion, after 1822 he served in Russian embassies across Western Europe, including in Vienna. He accurately predicted the Vienna Revolution of 1848, the abdication of Emperor Ferdinand, and the accession of Franz Joseph I.
In 1850, he first met Bismarck while handling the Prussian-Austrian dispute, supporting Austrian Chancellor Felix Schwarzenberg in pressuring Prussia to accept the Humiliation of Olmütz. During the
Crimean War
, as ambassador to the
Austrian Empire

, he foresaw that Britain and France would join the war and advised Tsar Nicholas I against pointless sacrifices, but his advice was not heeded. After the Crimean War, Nesselrode resigned as Foreign Minister, and in April 1856, Gorchakov became the new Foreign Minister. He immediately adopted a policy of reaffirming Russia's status as a European power and seeking friendly relations with France and Prussia. Although Russia, despite French protests, suppressed the Polish Kingdom Uprising in 1863, and he failed to maintain the restored friendly relations with France, he effectively conducted diplomacy with other European powers, securing public support from Prussia for Russia's actions.
In 1866, Tsar Alexander II appointed him Chancellor of the Empire as a reward. To enhance Russia's image, Gorchakov took advantage of Europe's preoccupation with the Franco-Prussian War in 1870 to declare the prohibitions imposed after the
Crimean War
—which forbade Russia from maintaining a fleet in the Black Sea and building fortifications on its coasts—null and void. He also facilitated the establishment of a loose defensive alliance between Russia, the German Empire, and Austria-Hungary (the Three Emperors' League, 1873). He dealt with Bismarck for nearly twenty years and was the only diplomat of the Bismarck era capable of rivaling him. Gorchakov was one of the few who comprehended Bismarck's intricate continental system, to the extent that the British Prime Minister felt a sense of dread and intense aversion whenever he heard of meetings between Bismarck and Gorchakov.
2

Despite these achievements, Gorchakov's role in determining Russian foreign policy began to decline in the mid-1870s. His personal antagonism with German Chancellor Otto von Bismarck caused the Three Emperors' League to fail to function as intended. His disapproval of Pan-Slavism could not prevent it from gaining significant influence in Russian foreign policy. Following the Bosnian Rebellion of 1875, his efforts to preserve the Three Emperors' League and maintain peace ended in complete failure. Furthermore, after the Tenth Russo-Turkish War of 1877-1878, he was unable to prevent his subordinate, Count Nikolay Pavlovich Ignatyev, from imposing the harsh Treaty of San Stefano on the defeated Ottoman Turks. He also failed to stop the intervention of the European powers, particularly British Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli, which led to the replacement of the Treaty of San Stefano with the Treaty of Berlin, a treaty far less favorable to Russia. Although he regarded the Treaty of Berlin as the greatest failure of his official career, he did not resign from his posts as Foreign Minister and Prime Minister until 1882.
Early Life
On October 19, 1811, twenty-nine noble youths aged 12 to 13, bathed in the dawn of a new era, entered the Tsarskoye Selo Lyceum, which had been established by order of Alexander I, to begin their six years of study. Among these twenty-nine individuals were Alexander Sergeyevich Pushkin, who would later become the great Russian poet; Wilhelm Küchelbecker, Volkhovsky, and Ivan Pushchin, who would later become Decembrists; and Alexander Mikhailovich Gorchakov, who would later become the Prime Minister of Russia.
In June 1817, the first cohort of students graduated from the Tsarskoye Selo Lyceum. As the top students in their class, Pushkin and Gorchakov were assigned to work in the Russian Foreign Ministry. Having left the stifling atmosphere of the Lyceum, they initially believed they had become birds released from a cage, free to enjoy happiness and liberty. However, upon entering the building situated by the Pevchesky Bridge in Saint Petersburg, they were nearly suffocated by the rampant bureaucracy and corruption within.

In November 1825, Tsar Alexander I died, and young officers seized the opportunity in December to stage an armed uprising; they demanded the establishment of constitutional democracy and the reform of Russia's serfdom. However, these uprisings, known as the "Decembrists," were not successful. The new Tsar, Nicholas I, brutally suppressed the rebellion, hanging five of its leaders and exiling over 120 individuals to Siberia, including Gorchakov's friend Ivan Pushchin. Gorchakov himself was not classified as a "Decembrist." Nevertheless, his connections with the "Decembrists" became known to the Tsar's close associates. After Pushchin died in exile due to illness, Gorchakov married Pushchin's widow, Alexandrovna, and took on the responsibility of supporting her and the four sons and one daughter she had with Pushchin. Although Alexandrovna's sister was a mistress of Nicholas I, the Tsar distrusted Gorchakov entirely. Within the Foreign Ministry, Gorchakov was labeled a "liberal," and his promotions were exceedingly slow.
Another reason for Gorchakov's lack of success in the Pevchesky Bridge Building was the predominance of officials of German descent within the Russian Foreign Ministry. The wife of Nicholas I was the daughter of the former Prussian King Frederick William III and the sister of the then Prussian King Frederick William IV. Due to this connection, numerous German diplomats who had been unsuccessful in their own country were hired to come to Russia, where they colluded with each other and gained control over the Pevchesky Bridge Building.
Karl Robert Nesselrode particularly detested talented Russians, and Gorchakov, as it happened, was arrogant due to his talent and full of self-admiration. Consequently, Nesselrode wrote in his assessment: "Not without ability, but does not love Russia!" Years later, when Gorchakov had risen to the position of master of the Pevchesky Bridge Building and saw this remark, he could neither laugh nor cry, and was unwilling to refute it with a single word.

The **House of Gorchakov**, or **Gortchakoff** (Russian: Горчако́в), is a Russian noble family claiming descent from Michael of Chernigov,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorchakov#cite_note-EB1911-1) although it did not gain prominence until the 18th century.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorchakov#cite_note-EB1911-1)

Prince **Aleksey Ivanovich** (1769–1817) served with distinction under his uncle Suvorov in the Turkish Wars, and took part as a general officer in the Italian and Swiss operations of 1799, and in the war against Napoleon in Poland in 1806–1807 (Battle of Heilsberg). He succeeded Barclay de Tolly as the Minister of War in 1813. His brother Andrei Ivanovich Gorchakov (1776–1855) was a general in the Russian army who took a conspicuous part in the final campaigns against Napoleon.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorchakov#cite_note-EB1911-1)
Prince **Peter Dmitrievich Gorchakov** (1790–1868) served under Mikhail Kamensky and Mikhail Kutuzov in the campaign against Turkey, and afterwards against France in 1813–1814. In 1820 he suppressed an insurrection in the Caucasus, for which service he was raised to the rank of major-general. In 1828–1829 he fought under Prince Peter von Wittgenstein against the Turks, won an action at Aidos, and signed the treaty of peace at Adrianople. In 1839 he was made governor of Eastern Siberia, and in 1851 retired into private life.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorchakov#cite_note-EB1911-1)

When the Crimean War broke out he offered his services to the emperor Nicholas, by whom he was appointed general of the VI army corps in the Crimea. He commanded the corps in the battles of Alma and Inkerman. He retired in 1855 and died at Moscow, on March 18, 1868.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorchakov#cite_note-EB1911-1)
Prince **Mikhail Dmitrievich** (1795–1861), brother of the last named, was appointed commander-in-chief of the Russian troops which occupied Moldavia and Wallachia after the outbreak of the Crimean War. In 1856 he was appointed governor-general of Poland in succession to Prince Paskevich. He died at Warsaw on May 30, 1861, and was buried, in accordance with his own wish, at Sevastopol.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorchakov#cite_note-EB1911-1)

## Alexander Gorchakov
[edit]
Prince **Alexander Mikhailovich Gorchakov** (1798–1883) served as Chancellor of the Russian Empire (in office from 1867) during the reign of Emperor Alexander II (r.1855–1881). He was educated at the Tsarskoye Selo Lyceum, where he had the poet Alexander Pushkin as a school-fellow.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorchakov#cite_note-EB1911-1) In 1820–22 he accompanied Foreign MinisterKarl Nesselrode to the Holy Alliance congresses at Troppau, Laibach, and Vienna._[citation needed_]
Gorchakov was appointed Foreign Minister in April 1856 soon after the end of the Crimean War of 1853 to 1856; he represented the Russian Empire at the Paris Congress of 1856. His main objective was to restore Russia's international prestige after the bitter defeat. At first he steered the country towards an alliance with Napoleon III of France, but rebuffed by the latter's support of the January Uprising in Poland, joined his archrival Otto von Bismarck in setting up the League of the Three Emperors in 1873. Following France's defeat in the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–1871, Gorchakov succeeded in his long-term goal or revising the key clauses of the Paris Treaty, especially those containing Russia's interests in the Black Sea._[citation needed_]
The aged chancellor was so disgusted by the modification of the Treaty of San Stefano at the Berlin Congress of 1878 that in 1882 he laid down all his offices and settled into retirement. He died some months later._[citation needed_]
The Gorchakov family play a central role in _1636: The Kremlin Games_ and other works in the Russian thread of the _1632_ alternate history science fiction series.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorchakov#cite_note-2)

## Alexander Gorchakov
[edit]
Prince **Alexander Mikhailovich Gorchakov** (1798–1883) served as Chancellor of the Russian Empire (in office from 1867) during the reign of Emperor Alexander II (r.1855–1881). He was educated at the Tsarskoye Selo Lyceum, where he had the poet Alexander Pushkin as a school-fellow.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorchakov#cite_note-EB1911-1) In 1820–22 he accompanied Foreign MinisterKarl Nesselrode to the Holy Alliance congresses at Troppau, Laibach, and Vienna._[citation needed_]
Gorchakov was appointed Foreign Minister in April 1856 soon after the end of the Crimean War of 1853 to 1856; he represented the Russian Empire at the Paris Congress of 1856. His main objective was to restore Russia's international prestige after the bitter defeat. At first he steered the country towards an alliance with Napoleon III of France, but rebuffed by the latter's support of the January Uprising in Poland, joined his archrival Otto von Bismarck in setting up the League of the Three Emperors in 1873. Following France's defeat in the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–1871, Gorchakov succeeded in his long-term goal or revising the key clauses of the Paris Treaty, especially those containing Russia's interests in the Black Sea._[citation needed_]
The aged chancellor was so disgusted by the modification of the Treaty of San Stefano at the Berlin Congress of 1878 that in 1882 he laid down all his offices and settled into retirement. He died some months later._[citation needed_]
The Gorchakov family play a central role in _1636: The Kremlin Games_ and other works in the Russian thread of the _1632_ alternate history science fiction series.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorchakov#cite_note-2)

## Early life and career
[edit]
Gorchakov was born at Haapsalu, Governorate of Estonia, and was educated at the Tsarskoye Selo Lyceum, where he had the poet Alexander Pushkin as a school-fellow. He became a good classical scholar, and learned to speak and write in French with facility and elegance. Pushkin in one of his poems described young Gorchakov as _Fortune's favoured son_, and predicted his success.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Gorchakov#cite_note-EB1911-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Gorchakov#cite_note-4)
On leaving the lyceum Gorchakov entered the foreign office under Count Nesselrode. His first diplomatic work of importance was the negotiation of a marriage between the Grand Duchess Olga and the crown prince Charles of Württemberg. He remained at Stuttgart for some years as Russian minister and confidential adviser of the crown princess. He foretold the outbreak of the revolutionary spirit in Germany and Austria, and was credited with counselling the abdication of Ferdinand I of Austria in favour of Francis Joseph. When the German Confederation was re-established in 1850 in place of the Frankfurt Parliament, Gorchakov was appointed Russian minister to the diet. It was here that he first met Count Bismarck, with whom he formed a friendship which was afterwards renewed at St Petersburg.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Gorchakov#cite_note-EB1911-3)

## Early life and career
The Emperor Nicholas found that his ambassador at Vienna, Baron Meyendorff, was not a sympathetic instrument for carrying out his schemes in the East. He therefore transferred Gorchakov to Vienna, where the latter remained through the critical period of the Crimean War. Gorchakov perceived that Russian designs against the Ottoman Empire, which was supported by Britain and France, were impracticable, and he counselled Russia to make no more useless sacrifices, but to accept the basis of a pacification. At the same time, although he attended the Paris conference of 1856, he purposely abstained from affixing his signature to the treaty of peace after that of Count Alexey Fyodorovich Orlov, Russia's chief representative. For the time, however, he made a virtue of necessity, and Alexander II, recognising the wisdom and courage which Gorchakov had exhibited, appointed him minister of foreign affairs in place of Count Nesselrode.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Gorchakov#cite_note-EB1911-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Gorchakov#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Gorchakov#cite_note-6)

## Minister of foreign affairs
[edit]
Not long after his accession to office, Gorchakov issued a circular to the foreign powers in which he announced that Russia proposed, for internal reasons, to keep herself as free as possible from complications abroad, and he added the now-historic phrase, _La Russie ne boude pas; elle se recueille_ ('Russia is not sulking, she is composing herself'). During the January Uprising in Congress Poland, Gorchakov rebuffed the suggestions of Britain, Austria and France for assuaging the severities employed in quelling it, and he was especially acrid in his replies to Earl Russell's despatches. The Prussian support was assured by the Alvensleben Convention. In July 1863 Gorchakov was appointed Chancellor of the Russian Empire, expressly in reward for his bold diplomatic attitude towards an indignant Europe. The appointment was hailed with enthusiasm in Russia.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Gorchakov#cite_note-EB1911-3)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Gorchakov#cite_note-%D0%AD%D0%A1%D0%91%D0%AD-7)
A rapprochement now began between the courts of Russia and Prussia, and in 1863, Gorchakov smoothed the way for the occupation of Schleswig-Holstein by German troops. That seemed equally favourable to Austria and Prussia, but it was the latter power that gained all the substantial advantages. When conflict arose between Austria and Prussia in 1866, Russia remained neutral and permitted Prussia to reap the benefits arising from the conflict and establish its supremacy in Germany.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Gorchakov#cite_note-EB1911-3)
In 1867 Russia and the United States concluded the sale of Alaska, a process which had begun as early as 1854 during the Crimean War. Gorchakov was not against the sale but always advocated for careful and secret negotiations and saw the eventuality of the sale but not the immediate necessity._[citation needed_]

## Gorchakov and Bismarck

By the preliminary peace of San Stefano, the Slavic aspirations seemed to be realised, but the stipulations of that peace were considerably modified by the Berlin Congress (13 June to 13 July 1878), at which the aged chancellor held nominally the post of first plenipotentiary, but left to the second plenipotentiary, Count Shuvalov, not only the task of defending Russian interests, but also the responsibility and odium for the concessions which Russia had to make to Britain and Austria. ## Gorchakov and Bismarck
Prince Gorchakov devoted himself entirely to foreign affairs, and took some part in the great internal reforms of Alexander II's reign: for example he submitted 4 projects of Emancipation reform and also presented to Alexander II analysis of foreign experience of various reforms. As a diplomatist he displayed many brilliant qualities: adroitness in negotiation, incisiveness in argument and elegance in style. His statesmanship, though marred occasionally by personal vanity and love of popular applause, was far-seeing and prudent. In the latter part of his career his main object was to raise the prestige of Russia by undoing the results of the Crimean War, and it may fairly be said that he in great measure succeeded.

He entered the diplomatic service in 1817 and attended international congresses in Troppau, Verona, and Laibach as a member of the official Russian delegation from 1820 to 1822. Despite efforts by Foreign Minister Count Karl Robert Nesselrode to block his promotion, after 1822 he served in Russian embassies across Western Europe, including in Vienna. He accurately predicted the Vienna Revolution of 1848, the abdication of Emperor Ferdinand, and the accession of Franz Joseph I.

, he foresaw that Britain and France would join the war and advised Tsar Nicholas I against pointless sacrifices, but his advice was not heeded. After the Crimean War, Nesselrode resigned as Foreign Minister, and in April 1856, Gorchakov became the new Foreign Minister. He immediately adopted a policy of reaffirming Russia's status as a European power and seeking friendly relations with France and Prussia. Although Russia, despite French protests, suppressed the Polish Kingdom Uprising in 1863, and he failed to maintain the restored friendly relations with France, he effectively conducted diplomacy with other European powers, securing public support from Prussia for Russia's actions.
In 1866, Tsar Alexander II appointed him Chancellor of the Empire as a reward. To enhance Russia's image, Gorchakov took advantage of Europe's preoccupation with the Franco-Prussian War in 1870 to declare the prohibitions imposed after the
Crimean War
—which forbade Russia from maintaining a fleet in the Black Sea and building fortifications on its coasts—null and void. He also facilitated the establishment of a loose defensive alliance between Russia, the German Empire, and Austria-Hungary (the Three Emperors' League, 1873). He dealt with Bismarck for nearly twenty years and was the only diplomat of the Bismarck era capable of rivaling him. Gorchakov was one of the few who comprehended Bismarck's intricate continental system, to the extent that the British Prime Minister felt a sense of dread and intense aversion whenever he heard of meetings between Bismarck and Gorchakov.

texts.2:
Despite these achievements, Gorchakov's role in determining Russian foreign policy began to decline in the mid-1870s. His personal antagonism with German Chancellor Otto von Bismarck caused the Three Emperors' League to fail to function as intended. His disapproval of Pan-Slavism could not prevent it from gaining significant influence in Russian foreign policy. Following the Bosnian Rebellion of 1875, his efforts to preserve the Three Emperors' League and maintain peace ended in complete failure. Furthermore, after the Tenth Russo-Turkish War of 1877-1878, he was unable to prevent his subordinate, Count Nikolay Pavlovich Ignatyev, from imposing the harsh Treaty of San Stefano on the defeated Ottoman Turks. He also failed to stop the intervention of the European powers, particularly British Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli, which led to the replacement of the Treaty of San Stefano with the Treaty of Berlin, a treaty far less favorable to Russia. Although he regarded the Treaty of Berlin as the greatest failure of his official career, he did not resign from his posts as Foreign Minister and Prime Minister until 1882.
Early Life
On October 19, 1811, twenty-nine noble youths aged 12 to 13, bathed in the dawn of a new era, entered the Tsarskoye Selo Lyceum, which had been established by order of Alexander I, to begin their six years of study. Among these twenty-nine individuals were Alexander Sergeyevich Pushkin, who would later become the great Russian poet; Wilhelm Küchelbecker, Volkhovsky, and Ivan Pushchin, who would later become Decembrists; and Alexander Mikhailovich Gorchakov, who would later become the Prime Minister of Russia.
In June 1817, the first cohort of students graduated from the Tsarskoye Selo Lyceum. As the top students in their class, Pushkin and Gorchakov were assigned to work in the Russian Foreign Ministry. Having left the stifling atmosphere of the Lyceum, they initially believed they had become birds released from a cage, free to enjoy happiness and liberty. However, upon entering the building situated by the Pevchesky Bridge in Saint Petersburg, they were nearly suffocated by the rampant bureaucracy and corruption within.
texts.3:
In November 1825, Tsar Alexander I died, and young officers seized the opportunity in December to stage an armed uprising; they demanded the establishment of constitutional democracy and the reform of Russia's serfdom. However, these uprisings, known as the "Decembrists," were not successful. The new Tsar, Nicholas I, brutally suppressed the rebellion, hanging five of its leaders and exiling over 120 individuals to Siberia, including Gorchakov's friend Ivan Pushchin. Gorchakov himself was not classified as a "Decembrist." Nevertheless, his connections with the "Decembrists" became known to the Tsar's close associates. After Pushchin died in exile due to illness, Gorchakov married Pushchin's widow, Alexandrovna, and took on the responsibility of supporting her and the four sons and one daughter she had with Pushchin. Although Alexandrovna's sister was a mistress of Nicholas I, the Tsar distrusted Gorchakov entirely. Within the Foreign Ministry, Gorchakov was labeled a "liberal," and his promotions were exceedingly slow.
Another reason for Gorchakov's lack of success in the Pevchesky Bridge Building was the predominance of officials of German descent within the Russian Foreign Ministry. The wife of Nicholas I was the daughter of the former Prussian King Frederick William III and the sister of the then Prussian King Frederick William IV. Due to this connection, numerous German diplomats who had been unsuccessful in their own country were hired to come to Russia, where they colluded with each other and gained control over the Pevchesky Bridge Building.
Karl Robert Nesselrode particularly detested talented Russians, and Gorchakov, as it happened, was arrogant due to his talent and full of self-admiration. Consequently, Nesselrode wrote in his assessment: "Not without ability, but does not love Russia!" Years later, when Gorchakov had risen to the position of master of the Pevchesky Bridge Building and saw this remark, he could neither laugh nor cry, and was unwilling to refute it with a single word.

**Dmitry Alekseyevich, Count Milyutin** (born June 28 [July 10, New Style], 1816, Moscow, Russia—died Jan. 25 [Feb. 7], 1912, Simeiz, near Yalta, Crimea, Russian Empire) was a Russian military officer and statesman who, as minister of war (1861–81), was responsible for the introduction of important military reforms in Russia.
Graduated from the Nicholas Military Academy in 1836, Milyutin served in the Caucasus (1838–45) and then became a professor at the academy. In 1856 Milyutin returned to active duty. In 1860 he entered the Ministry of War as deputy minister and became minister of war the following year. Milyutin reorganized the system of military education for both officers and regular troops; among other innovations, he made elementary education available to all draftees. In 1874 he introduced universal compulsory military service into Russia, compelling all Russian males at 20 years of age, except those who qualified for specific exemptions, to serve in the army; he also reduced the term of active service from 25 years to 6. In addition, Milyutin introduced the reserve system.
Despite the success of his reforms, which was demonstrated by Russia’s victory over the Ottoman Empire in the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–78, Milyutin acquired many powerful enemies, especially among those who resented his reduction of the nobles’ privileges within the military establishment. He chose to retire (May 1881) soon after Alexander III ascended the Russian throne.

## MILYUTIN, DMITRY ALEXEYEVICH
(1816–1912), count (1878), political and military figure, military historian, and Imperial Russian war minister (1861–1881).
General Adjutant Milyutin was born in Moscow, the scion of a Tver noble family. He completed the gymnasium at Moscow University (1832) and the Nicholas Military Academy (1836). After a brief period with the Guards' General Staff, he served from 1839 to 1840 with the Separate Caucasian Corps. While convalescing from wounds during 1840 and 1841, he traveled widely in Europe, where he decided to devote himself to the cause of reform in Russia. As a professor at the Nicholas Academy from 1845 to 1853, he founded the discipline of military statistics and provided the impulse for compilation of a military-statistical description of the Russian Empire. In 1852 and 1853 he published a prize-winning five-volume history of Generalissimo A. V. Suvorov's Italian campaign of 1799. As a member of the Imperial Russian Geographic Society he associated with a number of future reformers, including Konstantin Kavelin, P. P. Semenov-Tyan-Shansky, Nikolai Bunge, and his brother, Nikolai Milyutin. An opponent of serfdom, the future war minister freed his own peasants and subsequently (in 1856) wrote a tract advocating the liberation of Russian serfs.

## MILYUTIN, DMITRY ALEXEYEVICH
As a major general within the War Ministry during the Crimean War, Milyutin concluded that the army required fundamental reform. While serving from 1856 to 1860 as chief of staff for Prince Alexander Baryatinsky's Caucasian Corps, Milyutin directly influenced the successful outcome of the campaign against the rebellious mountaineer Shamil. After becoming War Minister in November 1861, Milyutin almost immediately submitted to Tsar Alexander II a report that outlined a program for comprehensive military reform. The objectives were to modernize the army, to restructure military administration at the center, and to create a territorial system of military districts for peacetime maintenance of the army. Although efficiency remained an important goal, Milyutin's reform legislation also revealed a humanitarian side: abolition of corporal punishment, creation of a modern military justice system, and a complete restructuring of the military-educational system to emphasize spiritual values and the welfare of the rank-and-file. These and related changes consumed the war minister's energies until capstone legislation of 1874 enacted a universal military service obligation. Often in the face of powerful opposition, Milyutin had orchestrated a grand achievement, although the acknowledged price included increased bureaucratic formalism and rigidity within the War Ministry.
Within a larger imperial context, Milyutin consistently advanced Russian geopolitical interests and objectives. He favored suppression of the Polish uprising of 1863–1864, supported the conquest of Central Asia, and advocated an activist policy in the Balkans. On the eve of the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878, he endorsed a military resolution of differences with Turkey, holding that the Eastern Question was primarily Russia's to decide. During the war itself, he accompanied the field army into the Balkans, where he counseled persistence at Plevna, asserting that successful resolution of the battle-turned-siege would serve as prelude to further victories. After the war, Milyutin became the _de facto_ arbiter of Russian foreign policy.

## MILYUTIN, DMITRY ALEXEYEVICH
Within Russia, after the Berlin Congress of 1878, Milyutin pressed for continuation of Alexander II's Great Reforms, supporting the liberal program of the Interior Ministry's Mikhail Loris-Melikov. However, after the accession of Alexander III and publication in May 1881 of an imperial manifesto reasserting autocratic authority, Milyutin retired to his Crimean estate. He continued to maintain an insightful diary and commenced his memoirs. The latter grew to embrace almost the entire history of nineteenth-century Russia, with important perspectives on the Russian Empire and contiguous lands and on its relations with Europe, Asia, and America.

W. Bruce Lincoln reflects on how Russian statesman Nikolay Milyutin became a chief architect of great liberal reforms.
One cold morning in early January 1837, two young men, carrying all their belongings in a few small cases, made their way along the banks of the Catherine Canal in St. Petersburg. The slighter of the two, a young man with deep-set eyes and sensitive features, was in an optimistic mood. For the first time since he had come to the Russian capital just over a year before, Nikolai Alekseevich Milyutin felt that fortune had turned her face toward him.
As a provincial secretary of the lowest rank in the Economic Department of the Russian Ministry of Interior, Nikolai Milyutin had just lived through one of the most unhappy years of his life. For the past twelve months, his days had been spent in a crowded office, buried deep in the recesses of one of the dark government buildings, where he and a host of other minor officials plied their routines.
As the northern winter, with its near-endless nights and dreary days, had approached, and as the damp winds from the Gulf of Finland had penetrated the walls of the poorly-heated rooms that he shared with a former schoolmate, Nikolai Svenchin, he had sunk deeper into despair. Indeed, it was a miserable life for a young man who placed a high value on his talents and aspired to become a great writer in the style of Schiller.
But a New Year’s gift of four-hundred rubles—even though they were paper, not the more valuable silver variety—seemed to hold forth the promise of better things. He and Svenchin were moving to warmer lodgings on the Catherine Canal and as he made his way against the cutting wind, Nikolai Milyutin was once again thinking great thoughts about what the future might bring.
Possibly he would now finish the manuscript of his play _Manfred_ upon which he had been labouring for more than three years, embark on a much-desired literary career, and leave behind for ever the dreary office where, as he wrote to his elder brother Dmitrii, an officer in the Russian army, ‘one only reads ignorant compositions, unravels knavish subterfuges, and struggles against illiteracy, intrigues, and stupidity.’

It is not surprising that Milyutin first sought to make his mark in the literary realm. Ever since he had entered the Boarding School for Sons of the Nobility in Moscow in 1829, he had cherished visions of a literary career, dreams that had been given added substance when his first play, _Amalat Bek_, an adolescent’s attempt to deal with ideas and literary forms which he did not fully comprehend, had been performed at the Boarding School theatre.
But, indeed, it was not as a playwright that Milyutin was to make his name known throughout Russia and much of Europe. After an inauspicious beginning, he rapidly ascended the rungs of the Russian bureaucracy and by early 1846, at the age of twenty-seven, he was well-launched on a brilliant career during which he would rise to become the central figure in drafting the emancipation of the Russian serfs in 1861 and the author of Russia’s new policy in Poland after the revolt of 1863.
Contrary to the view taken by historians who have written about mid-nineteenth-century Russian politics and society, Milyutin did not begin his studies of the peasant question, which would bring him international renown, until the beginning of Alexander II’s reign in 1855.
During his first twenty years of service in the Ministry of Interior, he had devoted his energy to a study of urban conditions in the Empire and he persistently advocated far-reaching reforms in Russian city government. His first efforts in this direction were soon crowned with success when, in 1846, he completed a reform plan for St. Petersburg which was to serve as a model for the Empire-wide Municipal Reform Law of 1870.
Milyutin’s work on the Petersburg municipal reform taught him some valuable lessons. Most important, he learned that in a highly stratified society, such as existed in Russia, it was necessary to rely upon the power of the autocrat to transcend the narrow interests of powerful conservative groups and protect the welfare of the entire state. In his view, only the Tsar, advised by progressive and knowledgeable counsellors, could bring about major reforms.
Yet Milyutin’s reliance on the power of the Tsar to bring about change was only one element of the enlightened outlook that set him apart from the mass of narrow-minded bureaucrats who thronged the government offices in mid-nineteenth-century Russia.

During his first two decades in the civil service, Milyutin had developed a responsible attitude toward state service which was shared by far too few of the officials in the Imperial government. Central to his view was the firm conviction that service to the state should not be regarded as an onerous burden, nor should it be viewed as a sinecure that could be exploited for one’s own interests.
Unlike most officials, who squandered their time and energy in intrigues to gain additional decorations or privileges, Milyutin would not serve simply for the attainment of personal ends. He served the state because he believed that it was his duty to serve honestly and efficiently. The welfare of the state as a whole became his major concern.
This attitude toward state service was perhaps best summarised by one of Milyutin’s closest friends, Andrei Zablotskii-Desyatovskii, who characterised the small group of officials who shared Milyutin’s outlook in the following way:
> ‘[These men] were not obsessed with a love of power, nor did they seek power for their own self-gratification. They were not consumed with a passion for wealth nor were they what are called careerists. Their ideal was the introduction of justice into all spheres of life.’
But although the reform of 1846 gained for Milyutin a considerable reputation, he had not yet acquired the breadth of outlook and sensitivity to the social and political consequences of change that is needed by those who bring about momentous changes in society.
He regarded the planning and execution of reforms as primarily an administrative problem in which progressive officials, armed with knowledge of local conditions, could bring about change if they were backed by the full power of the autocrat. His view of reform, then, was still the rather narrow one of a bureaucrat who favoured change.
During the late 1840’s and 1850’s, Milyutin’s views on reform were significantly broadened as the result of his new associations with the moderate intelligentsia in the Russian capital. His reputation as a reformer, earned because of his success in planning the Petersburg reform of 1846, gained him new popularity among the circles of the Petersburg intelligentsia.

As a regular visitor to some of their circles, Milyutin encountered men with more enlightened ideas than his own and, as a result, he rejected his earlier conception of change as an administrative measure in favour of a broader view of reform and its relationship to society.
Milyutin’s increasing identification with the outlook of the moderate intelligentsia occurred during one of the most oppressive periods that Russia’s intellectuals had to live through during the nineteenth century. Frightened by the wave of revolutions that swept western Europe in 1848, Nicholas I attempted to stifle any exchange of ideas, for he feared that any expression of independent opinion might lead to radical upheavals.
During the final years of his reign (184855) he expanded the state’s censorship machinery to such a degree that by 1850, according to the censor A. V. Nikitenko, there were no less than twelve separate organizations in the state bureaucracy devoted to the tasks of censorship. Not only were the writings of many western European writers declared illegal, but even the work of N. M. Karamzin, who had been the court historian in the early nineteenth century, suffered under the censor’s energetic pen.
During these difficult years between the revolutions of 1848 and the Crimean War, it became virtually impossible to exchange ideas in print in Russia. Further, the danger of discovery by the secret police made it difficult to discuss questions of reform even at private gatherings. It was for this reason that the salon of the Grand Duchess Elena Pavlovna, wife of the Tsar’s younger brother Grand Duke Mikhail Pavlovich, came to occupy a vital place in the lives of Milyutin and other progressive officials in St. Petersburg.
The victim of an unhappy marriage—her husband’s conduct toward her shocked even the other members of the Imperial family—Elena Pavlovna had turned to the study of books and ideas as an escape from the cares of her daily life. Unlike most of the Imperial family, she was intensely aware of the intellectual ferment then taking place in Russia, and her salon became one of the very few places in the capital where sensitive issues could be discussed with freedom.

**Nikolay Alekseyevich Milyutin** (born June 6 [June 18, New Style], 1818, Moscow, Russia—died Jan. 26 [Feb. 7], 1872, Moscow) was a Russian statesman who played a prominent role in the emancipation of the serfs in Russia.
Educated at Moscow University, Milyutin entered the Ministry of the Interior at the age of 17 and advanced rapidly in the service. In the early 1840s he was responsible for the reform of the municipal governments of St. Petersburg, Moscow, and Odessa. Appointed assistant minister of the interior in 1859, Milyutin took a leading part in the framing of the Emancipation Manifesto of March 3, 1861, from which he and his progressive associates succeeded in eliminating some of the more objectionable features advocated by the ultraconservative groups. He was forced to retire in April 1861, but, after the Polish insurrection of 1863, he was appointed secretary of state for the Russian part of Poland, where in 1864 he carried out the emancipation of the peasantry at the expense of the Polish landowners, whom he considered to be the core of Polish nationalism. Milyutin also removed all Roman Catholic priests and monks from Poland’s schools with a similar intent. He suffered a stroke in 1866 and lived in retirement thereafter.

**Nikolay Alekseyevich Milyutin** (born June 6 [June 18, New Style], 1818, Moscow, Russia—died Jan. 26 [Feb. 7], 1872, Moscow) was a Russian statesman who played a prominent role in the emancipation of the serfs in Russia.
Educated at Moscow University, Milyutin entered the Ministry of the Interior at the age of 17 and advanced rapidly in the service. In the early 1840s he was responsible for the reform of the municipal governments of St. Petersburg, Moscow, and Odessa. Appointed assistant minister of the interior in 1859, Milyutin took a leading part in the framing of the Emancipation Manifesto of March 3, 1861, from which he and his progressive associates succeeded in eliminating some of the more objectionable features advocated by the ultraconservative groups. He was forced to retire in April 1861, but, after the Polish insurrection of 1863, he was appointed secretary of state for the Russian part of Poland, where in 1864 he carried out the emancipation of the peasantry at the expense of the Polish landowners, whom he considered to be the core of Polish nationalism. Milyutin also removed all Roman Catholic priests and monks from Poland’s schools with a similar intent. He suffered a stroke in 1866 and lived in retirement thereafter.

W. Bruce Lincoln reflects on how Russian statesman Nikolay Milyutin became a chief architect of great liberal reforms.
One cold morning in early January 1837, two young men, carrying all their belongings in a few small cases, made their way along the banks of the Catherine Canal in St. Petersburg. The slighter of the two, a young man with deep-set eyes and sensitive features, was in an optimistic mood. For the first time since he had come to the Russian capital just over a year before, Nikolai Alekseevich Milyutin felt that fortune had turned her face toward him.
As a provincial secretary of the lowest rank in the Economic Department of the Russian Ministry of Interior, Nikolai Milyutin had just lived through one of the most unhappy years of his life. For the past twelve months, his days had been spent in a crowded office, buried deep in the recesses of one of the dark government buildings, where he and a host of other minor officials plied their routines.
As the northern winter, with its near-endless nights and dreary days, had approached, and as the damp winds from the Gulf of Finland had penetrated the walls of the poorly-heated rooms that he shared with a former schoolmate, Nikolai Svenchin, he had sunk deeper into despair. Indeed, it was a miserable life for a young man who placed a high value on his talents and aspired to become a great writer in the style of Schiller.
But a New Year’s gift of four-hundred rubles—even though they were paper, not the more valuable silver variety—seemed to hold forth the promise of better things. He and Svenchin were moving to warmer lodgings on the Catherine Canal and as he made his way against the cutting wind, Nikolai Milyutin was once again thinking great thoughts about what the future might bring.
Possibly he would now finish the manuscript of his play _Manfred_ upon which he had been labouring for more than three years, embark on a much-desired literary career, and leave behind for ever the dreary office where, as he wrote to his elder brother Dmitrii, an officer in the Russian army, ‘one only reads ignorant compositions, unravels knavish subterfuges, and struggles against illiteracy, intrigues, and stupidity.’
texts.1:
It is not surprising that Milyutin first sought to make his mark in the literary realm. Ever since he had entered the Boarding School for Sons of the Nobility in Moscow in 1829, he had cherished visions of a literary career, dreams that had been given added substance when his first play, _Amalat Bek_, an adolescent’s attempt to deal with ideas and literary forms which he did not fully comprehend, had been performed at the Boarding School theatre.
But, indeed, it was not as a playwright that Milyutin was to make his name known throughout Russia and much of Europe. After an inauspicious beginning, he rapidly ascended the rungs of the Russian bureaucracy and by early 1846, at the age of twenty-seven, he was well-launched on a brilliant career during which he would rise to become the central figure in drafting the emancipation of the Russian serfs in 1861 and the author of Russia’s new policy in Poland after the revolt of 1863.
Contrary to the view taken by historians who have written about mid-nineteenth-century Russian politics and society, Milyutin did not begin his studies of the peasant question, which would bring him international renown, until the beginning of Alexander II’s reign in 1855.
During his first twenty years of service in the Ministry of Interior, he had devoted his energy to a study of urban conditions in the Empire and he persistently advocated far-reaching reforms in Russian city government. His first efforts in this direction were soon crowned with success when, in 1846, he completed a reform plan for St. Petersburg which was to serve as a model for the Empire-wide Municipal Reform Law of 1870.
Milyutin’s work on the Petersburg municipal reform taught him some valuable lessons. Most important, he learned that in a highly stratified society, such as existed in Russia, it was necessary to rely upon the power of the autocrat to transcend the narrow interests of powerful conservative groups and protect the welfare of the entire state. In his view, only the Tsar, advised by progressive and knowledgeable counsellors, could bring about major reforms.
Yet Milyutin’s reliance on the power of the Tsar to bring about change was only one element of the enlightened outlook that set him apart from the mass of narrow-minded bureaucrats who thronged the government offices in mid-nineteenth-century Russia.
texts.2:
During his first two decades in the civil service, Milyutin had developed a responsible attitude toward state service which was shared by far too few of the officials in the Imperial government. Central to his view was the firm conviction that service to the state should not be regarded as an onerous burden, nor should it be viewed as a sinecure that could be exploited for one’s own interests.
Unlike most officials, who squandered their time and energy in intrigues to gain additional decorations or privileges, Milyutin would not serve simply for the attainment of personal ends. He served the state because he believed that it was his duty to serve honestly and efficiently. The welfare of the state as a whole became his major concern.
This attitude toward state service was perhaps best summarised by one of Milyutin’s closest friends, Andrei Zablotskii-Desyatovskii, who characterised the small group of officials who shared Milyutin’s outlook in the following way:
> ‘[These men] were not obsessed with a love of power, nor did they seek power for their own self-gratification. They were not consumed with a passion for wealth nor were they what are called careerists. Their ideal was the introduction of justice into all spheres of life.’
But although the reform of 1846 gained for Milyutin a considerable reputation, he had not yet acquired the breadth of outlook and sensitivity to the social and political consequences of change that is needed by those who bring about momentous changes in society.
He regarded the planning and execution of reforms as primarily an administrative problem in which progressive officials, armed with knowledge of local conditions, could bring about change if they were backed by the full power of the autocrat. His view of reform, then, was still the rather narrow one of a bureaucrat who favoured change.
During the late 1840’s and 1850’s, Milyutin’s views on reform were significantly broadened as the result of his new associations with the moderate intelligentsia in the Russian capital. His reputation as a reformer, earned because of his success in planning the Petersburg reform of 1846, gained him new popularity among the circles of the Petersburg intelligentsia.
texts.3:
As a regular visitor to some of their circles, Milyutin encountered men with more enlightened ideas than his own and, as a result, he rejected his earlier conception of change as an administrative measure in favour of a broader view of reform and its relationship to society.
Milyutin’s increasing identification with the outlook of the moderate intelligentsia occurred during one of the most oppressive periods that Russia’s intellectuals had to live through during the nineteenth century. Frightened by the wave of revolutions that swept western Europe in 1848, Nicholas I attempted to stifle any exchange of ideas, for he feared that any expression of independent opinion might lead to radical upheavals.
During the final years of his reign (184855) he expanded the state’s censorship machinery to such a degree that by 1850, according to the censor A. V. Nikitenko, there were no less than twelve separate organizations in the state bureaucracy devoted to the tasks of censorship. Not only were the writings of many western European writers declared illegal, but even the work of N. M. Karamzin, who had been the court historian in the early nineteenth century, suffered under the censor’s energetic pen.
During these difficult years between the revolutions of 1848 and the Crimean War, it became virtually impossible to exchange ideas in print in Russia. Further, the danger of discovery by the secret police made it difficult to discuss questions of reform even at private gatherings. It was for this reason that the salon of the Grand Duchess Elena Pavlovna, wife of the Tsar’s younger brother Grand Duke Mikhail Pavlovich, came to occupy a vital place in the lives of Milyutin and other progressive officials in St. Petersburg.
The victim of an unhappy marriage—her husband’s conduct toward her shocked even the other members of the Imperial family—Elena Pavlovna had turned to the study of books and ideas as an escape from the cares of her daily life. Unlike most of the Imperial family, she was intensely aware of the intellectual ferment then taking place in Russia, and her salon became one of the very few places in the capital where sensitive issues could be discussed with freedom.

**Dmitry Alekseyevich, Count Milyutin** (born June 28 [July 10, New Style], 1816, Moscow, Russia—died Jan. 25 [Feb. 7], 1912, Simeiz, near Yalta, Crimea, Russian Empire) was a Russian military officer and statesman who, as minister of war (1861–81), was responsible for the introduction of important military reforms in Russia.
Graduated from the Nicholas Military Academy in 1836, Milyutin served in the Caucasus (1838–45) and then became a professor at the academy. In 1856 Milyutin returned to active duty. In 1860 he entered the Ministry of War as deputy minister and became minister of war the following year. Milyutin reorganized the system of military education for both officers and regular troops; among other innovations, he made elementary education available to all draftees. In 1874 he introduced universal compulsory military service into Russia, compelling all Russian males at 20 years of age, except those who qualified for specific exemptions, to serve in the army; he also reduced the term of active service from 25 years to 6. In addition, Milyutin introduced the reserve system.
Despite the success of his reforms, which was demonstrated by Russia’s victory over the Ottoman Empire in the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–78, Milyutin acquired many powerful enemies, especially among those who resented his reduction of the nobles’ privileges within the military establishment. He chose to retire (May 1881) soon after Alexander III ascended the Russian throne.

## MILYUTIN, DMITRY ALEXEYEVICH
(1816–1912), count (1878), political and military figure, military historian, and Imperial Russian war minister (1861–1881).
General Adjutant Milyutin was born in Moscow, the scion of a Tver noble family. He completed the gymnasium at Moscow University (1832) and the Nicholas Military Academy (1836). After a brief period with the Guards' General Staff, he served from 1839 to 1840 with the Separate Caucasian Corps. While convalescing from wounds during 1840 and 1841, he traveled widely in Europe, where he decided to devote himself to the cause of reform in Russia. As a professor at the Nicholas Academy from 1845 to 1853, he founded the discipline of military statistics and provided the impulse for compilation of a military-statistical description of the Russian Empire. In 1852 and 1853 he published a prize-winning five-volume history of Generalissimo A. V. Suvorov's Italian campaign of 1799. As a member of the Imperial Russian Geographic Society he associated with a number of future reformers, including Konstantin Kavelin, P. P. Semenov-Tyan-Shansky, Nikolai Bunge, and his brother, Nikolai Milyutin. An opponent of serfdom, the future war minister freed his own peasants and subsequently (in 1856) wrote a tract advocating the liberation of Russian serfs.

## MILYUTIN, DMITRY ALEXEYEVICH
As a major general within the War Ministry during the Crimean War, Milyutin concluded that the army required fundamental reform. While serving from 1856 to 1860 as chief of staff for Prince Alexander Baryatinsky's Caucasian Corps, Milyutin directly influenced the successful outcome of the campaign against the rebellious mountaineer Shamil. After becoming War Minister in November 1861, Milyutin almost immediately submitted to Tsar Alexander II a report that outlined a program for comprehensive military reform. The objectives were to modernize the army, to restructure military administration at the center, and to create a territorial system of military districts for peacetime maintenance of the army. Although efficiency remained an important goal, Milyutin's reform legislation also revealed a humanitarian side: abolition of corporal punishment, creation of a modern military justice system, and a complete restructuring of the military-educational system to emphasize spiritual values and the welfare of the rank-and-file. These and related changes consumed the war minister's energies until capstone legislation of 1874 enacted a universal military service obligation. Often in the face of powerful opposition, Milyutin had orchestrated a grand achievement, although the acknowledged price included increased bureaucratic formalism and rigidity within the War Ministry.
Within a larger imperial context, Milyutin consistently advanced Russian geopolitical interests and objectives. He favored suppression of the Polish uprising of 1863–1864, supported the conquest of Central Asia, and advocated an activist policy in the Balkans. On the eve of the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878, he endorsed a military resolution of differences with Turkey, holding that the Eastern Question was primarily Russia's to decide. During the war itself, he accompanied the field army into the Balkans, where he counseled persistence at Plevna, asserting that successful resolution of the battle-turned-siege would serve as prelude to further victories. After the war, Milyutin became the _de facto_ arbiter of Russian foreign policy.

## MILYUTIN, DMITRY ALEXEYEVICH
Within Russia, after the Berlin Congress of 1878, Milyutin pressed for continuation of Alexander II's Great Reforms, supporting the liberal program of the Interior Ministry's Mikhail Loris-Melikov. However, after the accession of Alexander III and publication in May 1881 of an imperial manifesto reasserting autocratic authority, Milyutin retired to his Crimean estate. He continued to maintain an insightful diary and commenced his memoirs. The latter grew to embrace almost the entire history of nineteenth-century Russia, with important perspectives on the Russian Empire and contiguous lands and on its relations with Europe, Asia, and America.

## MILYUTIN, DMITRY ALEXEYEVICH
(1816–1912), count (1878), political and military figure, military historian, and Imperial Russian war minister (1861–1881).
General Adjutant Milyutin was born in Moscow, the scion of a Tver noble family. He completed the gymnasium at Moscow University (1832) and the Nicholas Military Academy (1836). After a brief period with the Guards' General Staff, he served from 1839 to 1840 with the Separate Caucasian Corps. While convalescing from wounds during 1840 and 1841, he traveled widely in Europe, where he decided to devote himself to the cause of reform in Russia. As a professor at the Nicholas Academy from 1845 to 1853, he founded the discipline of military statistics and provided the impulse for compilation of a military-statistical description of the Russian Empire. In 1852 and 1853 he published a prize-winning five-volume history of Generalissimo A. V. Suvorov's Italian campaign of 1799. As a member of the Imperial Russian Geographic Society he associated with a number of future reformers, including Konstantin Kavelin, P. P. Semenov-Tyan-Shansky, Nikolai Bunge, and his brother, Nikolai Milyutin. An opponent of serfdom, the future war minister freed his own peasants and subsequently (in 1856) wrote a tract advocating the liberation of Russian serfs.
texts.1:
## MILYUTIN, DMITRY ALEXEYEVICH
As a major general within the War Ministry during the Crimean War, Milyutin concluded that the army required fundamental reform. While serving from 1856 to 1860 as chief of staff for Prince Alexander Baryatinsky's Caucasian Corps, Milyutin directly influenced the successful outcome of the campaign against the rebellious mountaineer Shamil. After becoming War Minister in November 1861, Milyutin almost immediately submitted to Tsar Alexander II a report that outlined a program for comprehensive military reform. The objectives were to modernize the army, to restructure military administration at the center, and to create a territorial system of military districts for peacetime maintenance of the army. Although efficiency remained an important goal, Milyutin's reform legislation also revealed a humanitarian side: abolition of corporal punishment, creation of a modern military justice system, and a complete restructuring of the military-educational system to emphasize spiritual values and the welfare of the rank-and-file. These and related changes consumed the war minister's energies until capstone legislation of 1874 enacted a universal military service obligation. Often in the face of powerful opposition, Milyutin had orchestrated a grand achievement, although the acknowledged price included increased bureaucratic formalism and rigidity within the War Ministry.
Within a larger imperial context, Milyutin consistently advanced Russian geopolitical interests and objectives. He favored suppression of the Polish uprising of 1863–1864, supported the conquest of Central Asia, and advocated an activist policy in the Balkans. On the eve of the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878, he endorsed a military resolution of differences with Turkey, holding that the Eastern Question was primarily Russia's to decide. During the war itself, he accompanied the field army into the Balkans, where he counseled persistence at Plevna, asserting that successful resolution of the battle-turned-siege would serve as prelude to further victories. After the war, Milyutin became the _de facto_ arbiter of Russian foreign policy.
texts.2:
## MILYUTIN, DMITRY ALEXEYEVICH
Within Russia, after the Berlin Congress of 1878, Milyutin pressed for continuation of Alexander II's Great Reforms, supporting the liberal program of the Interior Ministry's Mikhail Loris-Melikov. However, after the accession of Alexander III and publication in May 1881 of an imperial manifesto reasserting autocratic authority, Milyutin retired to his Crimean estate. He continued to maintain an insightful diary and commenced his memoirs. The latter grew to embrace almost the entire history of nineteenth-century Russia, with important perspectives on the Russian Empire and contiguous lands and on its relations with Europe, Asia, and America.

**Dmitry Alekseyevich, Count Milyutin** (born June 28 [July 10, New Style], 1816, Moscow, Russia—died Jan. 25 [Feb. 7], 1912, Simeiz, near Yalta, Crimea, Russian Empire) was a Russian military officer and statesman who, as minister of war (1861–81), was responsible for the introduction of important military reforms in Russia.
Graduated from the Nicholas Military Academy in 1836, Milyutin served in the Caucasus (1838–45) and then became a professor at the academy. In 1856 Milyutin returned to active duty. In 1860 he entered the Ministry of War as deputy minister and became minister of war the following year. Milyutin reorganized the system of military education for both officers and regular troops; among other innovations, he made elementary education available to all draftees. In 1874 he introduced universal compulsory military service into Russia, compelling all Russian males at 20 years of age, except those who qualified for specific exemptions, to serve in the army; he also reduced the term of active service from 25 years to 6. In addition, Milyutin introduced the reserve system.
Despite the success of his reforms, which was demonstrated by Russia’s victory over the Ottoman Empire in the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–78, Milyutin acquired many powerful enemies, especially among those who resented his reduction of the nobles’ privileges within the military establishment. He chose to retire (May 1881) soon after Alexander III ascended the Russian throne.

**Sergey Yulyevich, Count Witte** (born June 29 [June 17, old style], 1849, Tiflis, Georgia, Russian Empire—died March 13 [Feb. 28, O.S.], 1915, Petrograd) was a Russian minister of finance (1892–1903) and the first constitutional prime minister of the Russian Empire (1905–06), who sought to wed firm authoritarian rule to modernization along Western lines.

## Life.
Witte’s father, of Dutch ancestry, directed the agricultural department in the office of the governor general of the Caucasus. His mother came from a high-ranking family of the Russian nobility engaged in state service. Witte’s childhood in the Caucasus was a happy one. Following his successful career as a student of mathematics at the Novorossiysky University (now Odessa State University) at Odessa, Witte thought of entering on an academic career. But he followed the advice of a family friend, the minister of communications, and entered the railway administration. It was the beginning of a career that brought Witte to the heart of imperial politics and finance. After a period in the chancellery of the governor general of Odessa and Bessarabia (1871–74), Witte studied railway administration in the Odessa Railway at the Odessa office of the Ministry of Communications. He led a disciplined, orderly life, imposed partly by family poverty and partly by an urge to succeed. By the time of the Russo-Turkish War (1877–78) he had already risen to a position in which he controlled all the traffic passing to the front along the lines of the Odessa Railway. At one critical point he devised a novel system of double-shift working to overcome delays on the line.
Witte showed his freedom from bureaucratic prejudice by appointing men of all nationalities—Jews, Poles, Ukrainians—as his subordinates and by cultivating favourable press relations. His economic acumen was shown in his collection and use of railway statistics and in the implementation of an effective freight tariff whereby he lowered freight rates and increased revenue.

## Life.
In 1889 Witte was invited to establish a railway department in the Ministry of Finance. He advanced rapidly and became in quick succession minister of communications (February 1892) and minister of finance (August 1892). Far-reaching plans for the economic development of the Russian Empire formed the kernel of Witte’s policy. He aimed at “removing the unfavourable conditions which hamper the economic development of the country and at kindling a healthy spirit of enterprise” (Witte’s first budget to the Emperor, 1893). Using the full power of the state, Witte unfolded a vast range of activity: a remodelled State Bank made ready capital available to industry; Russian steamship companies and nautical and engineering schools were established; savings banks were encouraged; company law was reformed; and the ruble was made convertible. Witte was also instrumental in raising large loans from investors in France, Britain, Belgium, and Germany to finance Russian industrialization.
He deployed his greatest energy in stimulating railway building, particularly the Trans-Siberian line (actually begun in 1891). He saw it not only as a means to bring urban progress to the countryside but also as an economic stimulus in itself, as a link between European and Asiatic Russia, and as a way of making Russia the chief intermediary between western Europe and the Far East. For almost a decade the “Witte system” enjoyed considerable success, but at the turn of the century international uncertainty (the South African [Boer] War, the Spanish–American War, and the Boxer Rebellion in China) reduced the flow of foreign loans to Russia, and strikes and peasant unrest in Russia revealed that the mass of the population would no longer tolerate the reduced living standards that Witte’s policy entailed. Moreover, influential agricultural interests, always hostile to Witte’s all-out support for industrialization, made their opposition manifest at court. His relationship with Emperor Nicholas II, who feared this dynamic man, was also unhappy. In August 1903 Witte was removed from the Ministry of Finance and appointed to the largely decorative position of chairman of the Committee of Ministers.

## Life.
He had to look on in impotence as the government blundered into war with Japan. But he was to render highly important services to the empire in 1905 and 1906. In July 1905 he was appointed chief Russian plenipotentiary to conduct peace negotiations with Japan. He obtained unexpectedly favourable terms for Russia, but his achievement did not make him any more popular.
At a political level, Witte, though he detested constitutionalism in any form, used his influence to persuade the Tsar to issue the “October Manifesto” of 1905, which promised to grant a measure of representative government. No less important was Witte’s role as prime minister in the new system of government, in organizing the repression of all the forces of disruption in the autumn and winter of 1905–06—_e.g.,_ the St. Petersburg Soviet, or workers’ council, the troop mutinies in the Far East, strikes in South Russia, and peasant uprisings in the Baltic provinces.

Witte was also instrumental in concluding arrangements in 1906 with a group of European bankers for a series of loans that restored Russian finances, which were in a state of virtual collapse through the effects of defeat in the Far East and the widespread revolts of 1905.
This was Witte’s last opportunity to serve the state. He was forced to resign the premiership in April 1906, having lost what little confidence the Tsar had in him. Witte never returned to office, and his efforts to influence policy were ineffectual. Thus, in the summer and winter of 1914–15 he vainly opposed Russian entry into World War I and was sympathetic to peace feelers put out by the German government through Witte’s own German banker. He died embittered and dispirited, foreseeing disaster for the tsarist empire.
